items.case: for permanent states and repeated or habitual actions
examples: Tom is a student. He goes to school every day.
He usually goes to school by bus.

items.case: for actions which finished at a stated time in the past
examples: He bought a new car last week.

items.case: for recent actions or states, or for actions which happened at an unstated time in the past
examples: I have bought a new bicycle.
items.hint: When did he buy it? We don't know. — unstated time

items.case: for actions or states which began in the past and continue up to the present
examples: I have been a teacher for two years.
items.hint: He is still a teacher.

items.case: completed action which happened at an unstated time in the past
examples: Don has left for Madrid.
items.hint: We don't know when he left; he's either there now or on his way there.

items.case: action which happened in the past and may be repeated
examples: I've spoken to Julia Roberts.
items.hint: I may speak to her again. She's alive — period of time not finished yet.

items.case: for actions or states which finished at a stated time in the past
examples: I bought this bicycle five years ago.
items.hint: When did he buy it? Five years ago. — stated time

items.case: for actions or states which finished in the past
examples: I was a student fourteen years ago.
items.hint: He isn't a student now. He is a teacher.

items.case: completed action which happened at a stated time in the past
examples: She left yesterday.
items.hint: When did she leave? Yesterday.

items.case: action which happened in the past and cannot be repeated
examples: I met Princess Diana.
items.hint: I won't meet her again. She's dead — period of time finished.

items.case: for an action which was in progress at a stated time in the past
examples: The girls were playing volleyball at five o'clock in the afternoon.
items.hint: When did they start? We don't know.

items.case: for two or more actions happening at the same time in the past
examples: The children were studying while their mother was cooking.

items.case: for an action which was in progress when another action interrupted it
examples: Mary was cooking when he burnt her hand.
items.hint: The action that interrupted it is in the past simple.

items.case: to describe the background to the events in a story
examples: We were walking in the woods. It was raining hard ...

items.case: for an action that took place at a specific time in the past
examples: Simon went to camp last month.
items.hint: When did he go to camp? Last month.

items.case: for actions which happened immediately one after the other in the past
examples: First she made the pizza, then she put it in the oven.
He slipped, fell over and hurt his ankle.

items.case: with non-continuous verbs
examples: Sylvia saw Alex at the party yesterday.
items.hint: appear (= seem), believe, belong, cost, feel, forget, hate, have (= possess), know, like, love, mean, need, prefer, realise, remember, see, seem, smell, sound, suppose, taste, think, understand, want, etc.

items.case: for people who are no longer alive
examples: Shakespeare wrote a lot of plays.
items.hint: Shakespeare is dead. He won't write any more.

cards.title: Past Perfect vs Past Perfect Continuous

items.case: for an action which happened before another past action or before a stated time in the past
examples: They had already reserved the table when they went to the restaurant.
They had already sat down for dinner by 8 pm.
items.hint: They made a reservation first and then they went to the restaurant.

items.case: for an action which finished in the past and whose result was visible in the past
examples: Bill had injured his legs in a car accident, so he had to use a wheelchair for six months.
items.hint: The action finished in the past and its result was visible in the past, too.

items.case: the past equivalent of the present perfect
examples: He had broken his leg, so he couldn't walk.
He has broken his leg, so he can't walk.
items.hint: In the first sentence the result was visible in the past; in the second it is still visible in the present.

items.case: to put emphasis on the duration of an action which started and finished in the past before another past action or a stated time in the past, usually with since or for
examples: They had been skating together for five years before they entered the competition.

items.case: for an action which lasted for some time in the past and whose result was visible in the past
examples: She had been working hard that day, so she was tired.
items.hint: She spent all day working hard and the result of the action was visible in the past, too.

items.case: the past equivalent of the present perfect continuous
examples: He had been waiting for hours, so he was bored.
He has been waiting for hours, so he is bored.
items.hint: In the first sentence the result was visible in the past; in the second it is still visible in the present.

blocks.heading: NOTE
items: We can use the past perfect or the past simple with before or after without any difference in meaning. She left after she had finished her work. / She left after she finished her work.

items.case: to talk about things we are not sure about or we haven't decided yet
examples: I'll probably buy a new bike.
items.hint: I'm not sure yet.

items.case: to express hopes, fears, threats, on-the-spot decisions, offers, promises, warnings, predictions, comments, etc. especially with expect, hope, believe, I'm afraid, I'm sure, I know, I think, probably
examples: I'm hungry. I'll make a sandwich.
It's cold. I'll close the window.
items.hint: on-the-spot decision

items.case: to make a prediction based on what we think or imagine
examples: I think you will pass the test.
She will probably phone later.
He will probably win the race.

items.case: to talk about actions which will definitely happen in the future and which we cannot control
examples: He will be twelve next year.
She will be twelve next month.

items.case: to talk about things we are sure about or we have already decided to do in the near future
examples: I'm going to buy a new bike.
He is going to fly to Rome tomorrow.
items.hint: I've decided it.

items.case: to express intentions and plans
examples: Now that I've got the money, I'm going to buy a new dress.
I'm going to get some more training so I can get a better job.
He likes acting. He is going to be an actor.
items.hint: intention / plan

items.case: when we can see evidence that something is going to happen
examples: Watch out! We're going to have an accident.
It's going to rain.
Watch out! You're going to fall.
items.hint: We can see a car coming. We can see dark clouds in the sky.

blocks.heading: TIME EXPRESSIONS USED WITH WILL AND BE GOING TO
